source.title: Memory Layers at Scale
source.authors: Vincent-Pierre Berges; Barlas Oğuz; Daniel Haziza; Wen-Tau Yih; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Gargi Ghosh

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures downstream task results across memory sizes and training-token amounts, and compares model-architecture ablations, using a different setup from the cited dense-model scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit or test held-out pretraining-loss power laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its task NLL and downstream benchmark results bear on downstream scaling and architecture sensitivity. Values used only to motivate engineering or modeling choices are not recorded.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, memory-augmented Llama-style models, the study reports downstream QA scores and task NLL as memory size grows (Fig. 1) and as training tokens grow from 200B to 1T (Table 2), for dense and Memory+ 8B models. It also runs fixed-size memory configuration ablations with training-set NLL (Tables 3–4). It fits no pretraining-loss power laws and no compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that memory layers add parameters without adding FLOPs, and that memory-augmented models beat dense models with more than twice the compute and beat compute- and parameter-matched MOE, especially on factual QA. They say factual QA improves predictably as memory scales to 128B parameters. They also say the gains are larger early in training, and they advocate memory layers for next-generation architectures.
record.recipe_differences: The study augments transformers by replacing selected feed-forward layers with shared trainable memory layers, then measures downstream tasks and architecture ablations; it does not reproduce the original dense-model loss-scaling or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with the number and placement of memory layers; the authors report an approximate sweet spot around 3 memory layers. They also vary value dimension and number of values.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched FLOPs, Memory+ models beat dense models with 2–4x more compute and beat parameter-matched MOE on QA (e.g. 1.3b NQ: Memory+ 13.68, MOE 8.14, dense 7.76).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding sparse memory parameters shifts downstream scaling curves at fixed compute; parameter count alone does not determine downstream performance across architectures.

record.problems: Figure 1 values are available only as plots in the supplied text. The ablation loss metrics are described as training-set log likelihood, not held-out pretraining loss. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for the cataloged results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 results for OBQA and PIQA and the Llama3.1 8B reference row are omitted. Table 1 and Figure 4 contain additional benchmark comparisons across base-model sizes; those results are not separately extracted here. Table 3 right-hand memory-mechanism variants and Table 4 right-hand key-dimension variants are omitted because they do not directly test fixed-parameter architecture-shape sensitivity. Table 2 values for the included metrics are reported for both Memory+ and dense checkpoints at both token amounts.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining-loss power-law fit in N, D or C.
No extrapolation from fitted small runs.
Dense depth/width shape at fixed parameters is not varied; only memory-layer configuration details are.
No other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No fitted functional form, no downstream-vs-pretraining-loss relation, and only two token points (200B, 1T) for the 8B models.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Downstream QA across dense, MOE, PEER, Memory and Memory+ at base sizes 134m–1.3b (e.g. dense NQ 0.91→7.76, TQA 7.7→32.64). Dense downstream scaling with parameters is directly relevant to V6.
Numeric memory-size sweep for 1.3b Memory+ at 1m/4m/16m/64m values (TQA 42.89, 51.18, 58.67, 62.14). This gives numbers for the figure-only F1–F2.
Memory-variant ablations at fixed memory size (training NLL 2.06–2.11), which also bear on loss sensitivity to architecture details.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling laws' in the paper are downstream scaling plots, not fitted power laws. Training NLL in the ablations is training-set loss at sub-1T budgets. The Table 4 text is garbled, so the D-row value-to-config mapping should be checked against the PDF. The paper's claim that more than 3 memory layers degrades performance is not visible in the training NLL (all 2.11).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss as a power law of parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit on small runs is extrapolated to larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter count versus training-token count is reported.
The ablations cover selected memory-layer placements and value dimensions, not a broad range of dense-transformer depth and width configurations.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
The study reports selected downstream benchmarks, not a general fit relating downstream performance to pretraining loss or a prediction law across model families.
The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or fitting choices, nor test whether curves depart from a single power law.
